label: Bonus Class 1
title: Every Word Has a Job: Parts of Speech
bigIdea: Every word in a sentence has a job (noun, verb, adjective, pronoun, preposition), and every English sentence needs a verb, even when Arabic does not: He is a teacher, not He teacher.
bigIdeaAr: لكل كلمة في الجملة وظيفة (اسم، فعل، صفة، ضمير، حرف جر)، وكل جملة إنجليزية تحتاج إلى فعل حتى عندما لا تحتاجه العربية: He is a teacher وليس He teacher.
builtOn: Lessons 1-2: Present Simple (I/you/we/they and he/she/it + -s): We hang out. She plays basketball.
Lesson 3: Present Simple negatives and opinion adjectives: I don't like boring shows. This game is awesome.
Lesson 4: There is / There are and room words: There is a lamp on my desk.

objectives.en: I can name five word jobs in English: noun, verb, adjective, pronoun and preposition.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أسمّي خمس وظائف للكلمات في الإنجليزية: الاسم، الفعل، الصفة، الضمير، حرف الجر.

objectives.en: I can find the verb in any English sentence.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أجد الفعل في أي جملة إنجليزية.

objectives.en: I can compare English word classes with Arabic اسم وفعل وحرف.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أقارن أقسام الكلام في الإنجليزية بالاسم والفعل والحرف في العربية.

objectives.en: I can fix sentences with a missing verb (He teacher -> He is a teacher).
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أصحّح جملاً ينقصها فعل (He teacher ← He is a teacher).

keyTerms.meaning: A word for a person, place, thing or idea: crew, desk, joke, Omar.
A word for an action or a state: chat, play, laugh, is, are, like.
A word that describes a noun: awesome, boring, weird, big.
A word that stands in for a noun: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
A small word that shows place or connection: on, in, under, by, with.
The group a word belongs to because of the job it does in a sentence.

linguisticsCorner.title: Word classes: the building blocks of every language
linguisticsCorner.titleAr: أقسام الكلام: حجارة البناء في كل لغة

facts.en: Almost every language in the world has at least two big word classes: nouns (things) and verbs (actions). Most linguists think this is one of the few near-universal features of human language, though a few languages are still debated.
facts.ar: تكاد كل لغات العالم تملك على الأقل قسمين كبيرين من الكلمات: الأسماء (الأشياء) والأفعال (الأحداث). ويرى معظم اللغويين أن هذا من الصفات القليلة المشتركة بين اللغات البشرية كلها تقريباً، مع أن بعض اللغات ما زال موضع نقاش.

facts.en: Arabic grammarians, like Sibawayh more than 1,200 years ago, divided words into three classes: اسم (noun), فعل (verb) and حرف (particle). Greek grammarians, about 2,000 years ago, used eight. Traditional English school grammar also uses eight parts of speech, but with a slightly different list.
facts.ar: قسّم علماء النحو العرب، مثل سيبويه قبل أكثر من 1200 سنة، الكلام إلى ثلاثة أقسام: اسم وفعل وحرف. أما نحويو اليونان قبل نحو 2000 سنة فقد استعملوا ثمانية أقسام، والنحو المدرسي الإنجليزي التقليدي يستعمل ثمانية أيضاً، لكن القائمة مختلفة قليلاً.

facts.en: A word's class depends on its job, not only on the word. In English the same word can change job with no change in form: I text my crew (verb) / I got a text (noun). Linguists call this conversion.
facts.ar: قسم الكلمة يعتمد على وظيفتها في الجملة وليس على شكلها فقط. في الإنجليزية قد تغيّر الكلمة وظيفتها دون أن يتغيّر شكلها: I text my crew (فعل) / I got a text (اسم). يسمّي اللغويون هذا التحويل (conversion).

facts.en: Nonsense test: in 'The blorks zibbed under the frim desk', you can tell that blorks is a noun, zibbed is a verb and frim is probably an adjective, even though the words are not real. Your brain uses position and endings as clues.
facts.ar: اختبار الكلمات المخترعة: في جملة 'The blorks zibbed under the frim desk' تعرف أن blorks اسم و zibbed فعل و frim صفة على الأرجح، مع أنها كلمات غير حقيقية. دماغك يستعمل موقع الكلمة ونهايتها دليلاً على وظيفتها.

arabicBridge.point: In traditional Arabic grammar, nouns, adjectives and pronouns are all اسم. English gives each of them its own class.
arabicBridge.pointAr: في النحو العربي التقليدي، الاسم والصفة والضمير كلها تدخل تحت قسم الاسم، أما الإنجليزية فتجعل لكل منها قسماً خاصاً.

arabicBridge.point: Same idea in both languages: a word for an action or event, with time inside it (play / يلعب).
arabicBridge.pointAr: الفكرة نفسها في اللغتين: كلمة تدل على حدث وفيها زمن (play / يلعب).

arabicBridge.point: English prepositions are close to Arabic حروف الجر. In Arabic, حرف also includes و (and), هل (a question marker) and لا (no / not). English puts and and not in other classes, and it has no single word like هل.
arabicBridge.pointAr: حروف الجر الإنجليزية قريبة من حروف الجر العربية، لكن قسم الحرف في العربية يضم أيضاً و وهل ولا، أما الإنجليزية فتضع and و not في أقسام أخرى، وليس فيها كلمة واحدة مثل هل.

arabicBridge.english: He is a teacher. / My room is big.
arabicBridge.point: An Arabic nominal sentence (الجملة الاسمية) like هو معلم needs no verb for 'is' in the present. English always needs a verb, so we add am / is / are.
arabicBridge.pointAr: الجملة الاسمية العربية مثل 'هو معلم' لا تحتاج في الحاضر إلى فعل بمعنى 'يكون'، أما الجملة الإنجليزية فتحتاج دائماً إلى فعل، لذلك نضيف am / is / are.

arabicBridge.english: He was a teacher. / He isn't a teacher.
arabicBridge.point: Arabic does use a 'be' verb in the past (كان) and, in Standard Arabic, in the present negative (ليس, which grammarians count as a verb, one of the sisters of كان). Only the present positive sentence has no verb. English uses be everywhere.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية تستعمل فعلاً بمعنى 'يكون' في الماضي (كان)، وفي نفي الحاضر في الفصحى (ليس، وهي فعل جامد من أخوات كان). الجملة الحاضرة المثبتة وحدها بلا فعل، أما الإنجليزية فتستعمل be في كل الحالات.

arabicBridge.english: There is a lamp on my desk.
arabicBridge.arabic: يوجد مصباح على مكتبي. / على مكتبي مصباح.
arabicBridge.point: Arabic can start with the place and use no verb; English needs the frame There is / There are.
arabicBridge.pointAr: العربية قد تبدأ بالمكان دون فعل، أما الإنجليزية فتحتاج إلى There is / There are.

commonErrors.why: Direct copy of هو معلم: Arabic present sentences like this need no verb for 'is'. English needs is (and a before a job).
Same nominal sentence pattern (غرفتي كبيرة جداً). Adjectives cannot be the verb in English.
Missing be before an adjective; the sentence has no verb.

commonErrors.wrong: I am play football every day.
commonErrors.why: Some students treat 'am' as a sign of 'present' and add it to every sentence. Play is already the verb; two verbs crash.
Same overuse of is. Like is the verb here; with she it needs -s.

commonErrors.wrong: There is books on the shelf.
commonErrors.right: There are books on the shelf.
commonErrors.why: The verb must match the noun after it: one thing -> is, many things -> are.

teacher: Bonus Class 1 slides with the five Word Job colors: noun = blue, verb = red, adjective = green, pronoun = purple, preposition = orange
Word cards on the slide from Lessons 1-4: crew, chat, joke, laugh, meme, awesome, boring, weird, poster, shelf, desk, lamp, beanbag, on, in, under, by, he, she, they
A sentence-builder slide with empty colored slots
Teams annotation tools (pen / highlighter) switched on for students
student: Paper and colored pens or pencils (blue, red, green, purple, orange) - or any five colors
Five small paper cards: N (noun), V (verb), Adj (adjective), P (pronoun), Prep (preposition)

stages.name: Warm-up: The Nonsense Sentence
stages.method: Curiosity hook with an invented-word sentence (grammar intuition)
stages.purpose: Show students they already 'feel' word classes, even with words that do not exist.
teacherSays: Welcome to the Grammar Lab, crew! Today you are scientists. Our lab partner is Lumi.
Lumi sent us a weird message: 'The blorks zibbed under the frim desk.' None of these words are real!
Question: what is a blork? A thing, an action or a description? How do you know?
And zibbed? And frim? Write your guess in the chat: thing, action or description.
You knew it without a dictionary. That means your brain already knows grammar. Today we name what your brain knows.
teacherSaysAr: لومي أرسل لنا رسالة فيها كلمات غير حقيقية. هل تعرفون أيها شيء وأيها حدث وأيها وصف؟
عرفتم الجواب بدون قاموس! هذا يعني أن دماغكم يعرف القواعد. اليوم سنعطي أسماء لما يعرفه دماغكم.
studentsDo: Read the nonsense sentence aloud.
Type in the chat: blorks = thing / zibbed = action / frim = description.
Say one clue that helped (the -s on blorks, the -ed on zibbed, frim sits before desk).
tips: Do not explain yet; let them argue for 30 seconds. Curiosity is the goal.
Accept answers in Arabic: شيء، حدث، وصف.

stages.name: Discovery: Meet the Five Word Jobs
stages.nameAr: اكتشاف: تعرّف على وظائف الكلمات الخمس
stages.method: Guided discovery (inductive grammar) with color-coded sentences
stages.purpose: Students find the five word classes themselves from real Lesson 1-4 sentences, then get the names and colors.
teacherSays: Look at these five sentences from our lessons. Some words are blue, some red, some green, some purple, some orange.
1. 'We hang out after school.' 2. 'She plays basketball.' 3. 'This game is awesome.' 4. 'There is a lamp on my desk.' 5. 'He makes a funny joke.'
Look only at the BLUE words: school, basketball, game, lamp, desk, joke. What do they have in common? ... Yes! They are things or people. These are NOUNS.
Now the RED words: hang out, plays, is, makes. They tell us what happens or what is. These are VERBS.
GREEN: awesome, funny. They describe a noun. ADJECTIVES.
PURPLE: we, she, he. They stand in for a person's name. PRONOUNS.
ORANGE: after, on. Small words that show place or connection. PREPOSITIONS.
Find the rule: how many red words are in each sentence? ... At least one in every sentence! Remember this - it's the key to today.
teacherSaysAr: انظروا إلى الكلمات الزرقاء فقط. ما الشيء المشترك بينها؟ كلها أشياء أو أشخاص: هذه أسماء.
الكلمات الحمراء أفعال، والخضراء صفات، والبنفسجية ضمائر، والبرتقالية حروف جر.
لاحظوا: في كل جملة كلمة حمراء واحدة على الأقل. هذا هو سرّ درس اليوم.
studentsDo: Look at the color groups and say what each group has in common (English or Arabic).
Hold up the right card (N, V, Adj, P, Prep) when the teacher points to a word.
Count the red words in each sentence and notice every sentence has at least one.
Sort 10 new words into the five classes.

exercise.instructions: What is the word's job? Type N, V, Adj, P or Prep in the chat.
exercise.instructionsAr: ما وظيفة الكلمة؟ اكتب N أو V أو Adj أو P أو Prep في الدردشة.

tips: Let them find the pattern before you say the term. The name comes last.
Keep the colors identical in every Grammar Lab class: the colors become the group's shared language.
If a student says 'a noun is a thing', add 'or a person, a place or an idea' (Omar, school, joke).

stages.name: Linguistics Corner: Same Word, Different Job
stages.nameAr: ركن اللغويات: الكلمة نفسها بوظيفة مختلفة
stages.method: Mini-lecture with a puzzle (concept check through conversion)
stages.purpose: Understand that a word's class depends on its job in the sentence, and that word classes exist in all languages.
teacherSays: Fact: almost every language on Earth has nouns and verbs. Most linguists think it's one of the very few things nearly all languages share.
Old Arabic grammarians, like Sibawayh, used three classes: اسم، فعل، حرف. Old Greek grammarians used eight. English school grammar also uses eight, with a slightly different list.
Now a puzzle. 'I text my crew.' Is text a noun or a verb? ... Verb! 'I got a text.' Now? ... Noun!
Same word, different job. Linguists call this conversion. English does it all the time: chat, joke, text, laugh.
So how do you know? Look at the neighbors. After a / the / my -> probably a noun. After I / we / they -> probably a verb.
teacherSaysAr: كل لغات العالم تقريباً فيها أسماء وأفعال.
في الإنجليزية الكلمة نفسها قد تكون اسماً أو فعلاً حسب مكانها. انظر إلى الكلمة التي قبلها: بعد a / the / my غالباً اسم، وبعد I / we / they غالباً فعل.
studentsDo: Decide noun or verb for the same word in two sentences.
Explain the clue they used (the neighbor word).
Challenge: make your own pair with chat or joke.

exercise.instructions: Is the underlined word a noun or a verb here? Say the clue word that helped you.
exercise.instructionsAr: هل الكلمة المحددة اسم أم فعل هنا؟ اذكر الكلمة التي ساعدتك.

items.prompt: I text my crew every day. (text)
I got a text from Sara. (text)
Our group chat is so funny. (chat)

tips: Keep the history facts short; the puzzle is the real learning.
Arabic usually changes the form when the job changes (ضَحِكَ 'he laughed' / ضَحْكة 'a laugh'); English often keeps the same form. Mention only if students ask.

stages.name: Arabic Bridge: The Missing Verb
stages.purpose: Compare English classes with اسم/فعل/حرف and explain why English needs am / is / are where Arabic has no verb.
teacherSays: Arabic grammar has three classes: اسم، فعل، حرف. Where do our five English classes go? Nouns, adjectives and pronouns are all اسم in Arabic grammar. Prepositions are حروف جر.
Now look: هو معلم. How many verbs? ... Zero! It's a nominal sentence - جملة اسمية. Perfectly correct Arabic.
English: He teacher. Is there a red word? No! An English sentence without a verb is broken. English says: He IS a teacher.
Same with غرفتي كبيرة -> My room IS big. And النكتة مضحكة -> The joke IS funny.
Interesting: Arabic uses كان in the past: كان معلماً. And ليس in the present negative: ليس معلماً. So Arabic has no verb only in the present positive. English always needs one.
Rule of the Lab: every English sentence needs a red word.
teacherSaysAr: جملة 'هو معلم' جملة اسمية صحيحة تماماً في العربية، ولا فعل فيها.
لكن الجملة الإنجليزية بلا فعل جملة مكسورة، لذلك نقول He is a teacher.
العربية تستعمل كان في الماضي وليس في نفي الحاضر، ولا تخلو الجملة من الفعل إلا في الحاضر المثبت. أما الإنجليزية فتحتاج إلى الفعل دائماً.
studentsDo: Translate three short Arabic nominal sentences and spot where English needs is / are.
Say each English sentence and tap the table on the red word (is / are).
Compare: كان معلماً = He was a teacher; ليس معلماً = He isn't a teacher.

exercise.instructions: Say it in English. Remember the red word (am / is / are). Short forms (I'm, He's) are fine too.
exercise.instructionsAr: قلها بالإنجليزية، ولا تنسَ الكلمة الحمراء (am / is / are). ويمكنك استعمال الصيغ المختصرة مثل I'm و He's.

items.answer: The lamp is on the desk.
There is a poster on the wall.

tips: Say clearly that هو معلم is correct Arabic. The point is difference, not 'Arabic is missing something'.
Point out the article too: Arabic معلم -> English a teacher.

stages.name: Grammar Detective: Fix the Broken Sentences
stages.method: Error correction as a detective case (noticing + self-correction)
stages.purpose: Practice finding the verb and repairing typical Arabic-speaker sentences.
teacherSays: Detectives! Lumi's robot wrote these sentences, but some are broken. Your job: find the problem and fix it.
Step 1: find the red word. Step 2: no red word? Add one. Two crashing verbs? Remove one.
Careful - some sentences are already correct. Don't fix what isn't broken!
Noor, you're detective one. Read sentence 1. Is it broken?
teacherSaysAr: ابحثوا عن الفعل أولاً. إذا لم يوجد فأضيفوه، وإذا وُجد فعلان متصادمان فاحذفوا واحداً.
studentsDo: Take turns reading a sentence and deciding: correct or broken.
Type the fixed sentence in the chat.
Name the reason in one word: missing verb / two verbs / is or are.

exercise.instructions: Correct or broken? Fix the broken ones.
exercise.instructionsAr: صحيحة أم مكسورة؟ أصلح الجمل المكسورة.

items.answer: Omar is my best friend. (missing verb)
The beanbag is very soft. (missing verb)

items.prompt: I am chat with my crew every day.
items.answer: I chat with my crew every day. (two verbs)

items.prompt: There is two lamps in my room.
items.answer: There are two lamps in my room. (is/are)
The speaker is on the shelf. (missing verb)

items.prompt: There are a rug under my desk.
items.answer: There is a rug under my desk. (is/are)

tips: Praise the reason, not just the answer: 'missing verb' is real grammar thinking.
'I am chat' is a very common error: students think 'am' means 'present'. Say: 'chat is already your red word'.

stages.name: Team Challenge: Sentence Builder Race
stages.purpose: Produce correct sentences from word-class patterns, with a verb in every one.
teacherSays: Two teams: Team Omar and Team Sara. I show a color pattern. You build a true sentence about you that fits the pattern.
Example: purple - red - green: 'I am tired.' / 'We are awesome.'
One point for a correct sentence, one bonus point for the fastest team, and one bonus point for a funny sentence.
Golden rule: if there's no red word, no points!
teacherSaysAr: أعرض عليكم نمطاً من الألوان، وأنتم تبنون جملة صحيحة عن أنفسكم تطابق النمط.
studentsDo: Work in pairs (or alone in a group of 2) to build a sentence for each color pattern.
Type it in the chat or say it on the mic; the other team checks the colors.
Use words from Lessons 1-4: crew, joke, meme, shelf, desk, poster, awesome, weird, chat, laugh, text.

exercise.instructions: Build a sentence that matches the color pattern. (Model answers below - any correct sentence wins.)
exercise.instructionsAr: ابنِ جملة تطابق نمط الألوان. (إجابات نموذجية أدناه، وأي جملة صحيحة مقبولة.)

items.answer: We play football. / I text Noor.
She is funny. / They are awesome.
Lumi laughs at memes. / Books are on the shelf.
He has a weird nickname. / I like cool posters.
My room is small. / The joke is lame.
There is a lamp on my desk. / There are posters on the wall.
I don't like boring shows. / He doesn't watch lame movies.

items.prompt: Free choice: a sentence with all five colors
items.answer: She chats with her crew in a cool group chat. (pronoun, verb, preposition, adjective, noun)

tips: Show patterns as colored blocks, not words, so students must think in classes.
With 2 students, play student vs Lumi (the teacher plays Lumi and makes deliberate mistakes for them to catch).
Accept possessives (my, her) and articles (a, the) as 'helpers'; we do not score them as a color today.

stages.name: Exit Ticket, Did You Know? and Mission
stages.purpose: Check that each student can find the verb and fix a verbless sentence; send them home with a fact to share.
teacherSays: Exit ticket: five quick items. Work alone, type your answers in a private chat to me.
Did you know? Many languages - Arabic, Russian, Indonesian and others - can say 'He teacher' with no verb in the present. English is the strict one: it always wants a verb.
Your mission: explain to someone at home why English says 'He is a teacher' but Arabic says 'هو معلم'.
teacherSaysAr: هل تعلم؟ لغات كثيرة مثل العربية والروسية والإندونيسية تقول 'هو معلم' بلا فعل في الحاضر، أما الإنجليزية فصارمة: تريد فعلاً دائماً.
مهمتك: اشرح لأحد في البيت لماذا نقول He is a teacher بالإنجليزية.
studentsDo: Answer the 5 exit-ticket items in a private chat.
Say the big idea in one sentence (English or Arabic).
tips: Anyone who scores under 4/5: give them 2 'find the verb' sentences in the warm-up of Lesson 5.
Keep the Did You Know? fact for the start of Lesson 5 too: 'Who explained it at home?'

exitTicket.instructions: Answer quickly: name the word class or fix the sentence.
exitTicket.instructionsAr: أجب بسرعة: اذكر قسم الكلمة أو أصلح الجملة.

items.prompt: What class is 'awesome' in 'This game is awesome'?
Find the verb: 'My crew hangs out at the mall.'
Noun or verb? 'I got a text.' (text)
Fix it: 'There is three posters on the wall.'
items.answer: There are three posters on the wall.

homework.en: Color Detective: write 6 sentences about your room and your crew. Color every word: nouns blue, verbs red, adjectives green, pronouns purple, prepositions orange. Check that every sentence has a red word.
homework.ar: المحقق الملوّن: اكتب 6 جمل عن غرفتك وأصدقائك، ولوّن كل كلمة: الأسماء بالأزرق، والأفعال بالأحمر، والصفات بالأخضر، والضمائر بالبنفسجي، وحروف الجر بالبرتقالي. تأكد أن في كل جملة كلمة حمراء.
tasks: Write and color 6 sentences (3 about your room, 3 about your friends).
Write 2 Arabic nominal sentences (like هو معلم) and their English translations with is / are.
Find one word that can be both a noun and a verb (like text or chat) and write two sentences.

support: Start with only three classes (noun, verb, adjective), then add pronoun and preposition.
Give a word bank sorted by color for the Sentence Builder Race.
Let students answer with the card or color instead of the term.
challenge: Learn the other three English parts of speech: adverb (quickly), conjunction (and, but), interjection (wow!). Find one of each in a sentence.
Write a nonsense sentence like Lumi's and let the group label the classes.
Find a word that can be two classes with no change in form, like 'cool' (adjective: a cool jacket / verb: Let the tea cool.). Write a sentence for each job.

successCriteria: Sorts at least 8 of 10 words into the correct class.
Finds the verb in any Lesson 1-4 sentence.
Judges at least 8 of the 10 detective sentences correctly (2 are already correct) and names the reason for each fix.
Explains in English or Arabic why English needs is in He is a teacher.
watchFor: Missing be: He teacher / My room big / The meme funny
Extra be with a main verb: I am play / She is like
Confusing adjectives and nouns (awesome vs game)

teacherNotes: This class gives the group a shared metalanguage (noun, verb, adjective...) and five colors. Use the same colors in every lesson and Bonus Class after this.
Do not teach adverbs, conjunctions and interjections to the whole group today; they are a challenge item only.
Arabic is presented as a different system, not a wrong one. Students who know some Arabic grammar (مبتدأ وخبر) will enjoy the comparison; others only need 'Arabic can skip the verb, English can't'.
Bonus Class 2 builds on this: once students know the word classes, they learn the fixed order in which English puts them (S-V-O and adjective before noun).

deck.title: None of these words are real!
deck.big: The blorks zibbed under the frim desk.
deck.text: What is a blork? And zibbed? And frim? A thing, an action or a description?
deck.ar: لا توجد كلمة حقيقية هنا! أيها شيء، وأيها حدث، وأيها وصف؟

deck.instructions: Type your guess in the chat. Which clue helped you?
deck.instructionsAr: اكتب تخمينك في الدردشة. ما الدليل الذي ساعدك؟

deck.title: Every language has word jobs
deck.text: Almost every language has nouns and verbs. Sibawayh, more than 1,200 years ago, used three classes for Arabic. Old Greek grammar used eight, and English school grammar uses eight too.
deck.ar: كل اللغات تقريباً فيها أسماء وأفعال. قسّم سيبويه الكلام العربي إلى ثلاثة أقسام، واستعمل النحو اليوناني ثمانية.

deck.ribbon: Grammar lab · same word, new job
deck.title: Conversion: same word, different job
deck.big: I text my crew.  /  I got a text.
bullets: After a / the / my: probably a noun
After I / we / they: probably a verb
English does it all the time: chat, joke, text, laugh
deck.ar: الكلمة نفسها قد تكون اسماً أو فعلاً، فانظر إلى الكلمة التي قبلها.

deck.instructions: Noun or verb here? Say the clue word that helped you.
deck.instructionsAr: هل الكلمة اسم أم فعل هنا؟ اذكر الكلمة التي ساعدتك.

deck.title: Where do the five English jobs go in Arabic?
deck.note: Arabic حرف also covers words like و and هل. English puts and and not in other classes.
deck.noteAr: قسم الحرف في العربية يضم أيضاً و وهل ولا، أما الإنجليزية فتضع and و not في أقسام أخرى.

deck.title: Arabic can skip the verb. English can't!

deck.instructions: Say it in English. Remember the red word: am / is / are.

deck.ribbon: Did you know · the strict one
deck.text: Many languages, like Arabic, Russian and Indonesian, can say 'He teacher' with no verb in the present. English is the strict one: it always wants a verb.
deck.ar: العربية والروسية والإندونيسية تستغني عن الفعل في جملة مثل 'هو معلم'، أما الإنجليزية فتريد فعلاً دائماً.

items.q: In Arabic, هو معلم is a correct sentence with no verb.
items.qAr: جملة 'هو معلم' صحيحة في العربية ولا فعل فيها.
items.why: Yes! It is a nominal sentence. English needs is: He is a teacher.
